CONSENT CALENDAR

1.  Actions

  prepared for the Council’s approval.
  Recommended Action

2.  Warrants

  Recommended Action

  $1,364,876.19.

3.  Adopt an Ordinance Prohibiting Fireworks in the City of Avalon
  This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived at the May 19, 2026
  regular City Council Meeting. Though the City has already adopted the Los Angeles
  County Fire Code which prohibits fireworks
  —  —  in order to simplify enforcement, staff
  recommends adoption of a basic ordinance that prohibits the use, possession, sale and
  discharge of fireworks within the city without a permit.
  Recommended Action
  Adopt an ordinance prohibiting the use, possession, sale and discharge of fireworks
  within the City of Avalon.

4.  Award Professional Audit Services Contract
  The City issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) for professional auditing services. The
  City received three (3) proposals from firms meeting the mandatory elements outlined in
  the RFP.
  Recommended Action
  Authorize the City Manager to execute a professional services agreement with DavisFarr
  LLP for professional auditing services for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, with the
  option of extending for the two (2) subsequent fiscal years.

GENERAL BUSINESS

5.  Catalina Food Tours Transportation Permit Application
  On April 26, 2026, the City received a transportation permit application from Ms. Erin
  Eubank to conduct guided food tours utilizing one existing Residential Vehicle permit
  assigned to business partner Simon Alvarez. The existing company is a walking tour and
  would like to add a transportation component for local restaurants further out from town
  center.
  Recommended Action
  1. Receive presentation. 2. Discuss. 3. If consensus is met, approve the Transportation
  Permit for Catalina Food Tours to be added to the existing Residential Vehicle permit to
  conduct tours with stated conditions.

6.  Roger’s Guided Tours Transportation Permit Application
  On March 31, 2026, the City received a transportation permit application from Mr. Roger
  Cadman to conduct guided tours utilizing one existing Residential Autoette permit. The
  Residential Autoette would be used to conduct in-town tours.
  Recommended Action
  1. Receive presentation. 2. Discuss. 3. If consensus is met, approve the Transportation
  Permit for Roger’s Guided Tours utilizing one existing Residential Autoette permit to
  conduct tours with stated conditions.

7.  Pebbly Beach Road Temporary Turn Around Installation and Traffic Safety Improvements
  Due to construction associated with the Cabrillo Mole Revitalization Project, the parking
  and turn around area located at the Cabrillo Mole approximately 120 Pebbly Beach
  —

  Road will be eliminated. To support taxi and tour operations, as well as traffic safety for
  —

  all vehicles, City Staff have developed a plan to mitigate congestion.
  Recommended Action
  Approve the plan as presented for modifications and striping along Pebbly Beach Road
  including installation of k-rail, signage and striping to install a temporary vehicle turn
  around.

8.  Adult-Use Cannabis Discussion
  A member of the City Council requested City Staff bring back a discussion regarding
  expansion of the sale of adult-use/recreational cannabis in Avalon.
  Recommended Action
  Provide direction to Staff regarding City Council’s desire to pursue legalization of adult-
  use cannabis in Avalon.

  from Orange County Winwater Company utilizing Saltwater Fund 11325-6552 for

  Hearing Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste Fees; (3) Consider a Resolution to
  —

  Adopt Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste Fees; (4) Find the Fees Exempt from
  Review Under CEQA; and (5) Set Public Hearing for Collection of Fees on Tax
  Roll
  1. City Council adopted Resolution No. 26-16 of the City Council of the City of
  Avalon Adopting Findings and Determinations Related to the Presentment of
  Objections to the Proposed Sewer, Saltwater, and Solid Waste Service Fees.
  Motion to approve made by Michael Ponce, seconded by Lisa Lavelle. (All Ayes)

  2. Mayor Marshall opened the public hearing. Public comments were heard; Mayor
  Marshall closed the public hearing, and determined that written protests from the
  owners of a majority of the parcels subject to the proposed Sewer, Saltwater, and
  Solid Waste rate increases had not been received. A majority protest does not
  exist.

  3. City Council adopted Resolution No. 26-17 of the City Council of the City of
  Avalon Establishing Rates for Sewer, Saltwater, And Solid Waste Service Fees
  and Finding These Rates Are Exempt from the California Environmental Quality
  Act.

  4. The establishment of maximum service fees was found to be exempt from the
  California Environmental Quality Act (“CEQA”); and

  5. Following adoption of the Resolution by at least a two-thirds vote of the City
  Council, Staff was directed to schedule a new public hearing to adopt a report and
  direct placement of the annual fees for Fiscal Year 2026—2027 Sewer, Saltwater,
  and Solid Waste fees on the property tax roll by the County of Los Angeles.
  Motion to approve made by Lisa Lavelle, seconded by Michael Ponce. (All Ayes)

GENERAL BUSINESS

  possession, sale and discharge of fireworks within the City of Avalon.

  negotiate and bring back a contract agreement with Anderson Burton Construction

SUBJECT:  Adopt an Ordinance Prohibiting Fireworks in the City of Avalon

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Adopt an ordinance prohibiting the use, possession, sale and
discharge of fireworks within the City of Avalon.

REPORT SUMMARY: This ordinance was introduced and all further readings were waived at
the May 19, 2026 regular City Council Meeting.

Every year City of Avalon, LA County Fire and Sherriff personnel have problems with illegal
fireworks. Though the City has already adopted the Los Angeles County Fire Code which  —

prohibits fireworks — in order to simplify enforcement, staff recommends adoption of a basic
ordinance that prohibits the use, possession, sale and discharge of fireworks within the city.

The intent of the new ordinance is to reasonably regulate the possession, sale, use or discharge
of dangerous fireworks within the city to protect the public health, safety, property and general
welfare of its residents and visitors alike. Avalon is located in a “Very High Fire Severity Zone.”
Illegal discharge of fireworks can easily lead to a large-scale fire within the City.

The ordinance makes it unlawful for any person or responsible party to possess, sell, use or
discharge dangerous fireworks unless a permit authorizing such possession, sale, use or
discharge has been issued by the Fire Chief to the person or responsible party using, selling, or
discharging or found in possession of said fireworks, and unless such person is in possession
of a valid pyrotechnic operator’s license issued by the Office of the State Fire Marshal. The Fire
Chief may establish reasonable rules and regulations for governing issuance of a firework permit
and may issue the same subject to payment of a fee as established by the City Council.

In addition to prohibiting fireworks in Avalon, the proposed ordinance establishes penalties from
$250 to $1 000 for each violation of the ordinance.

Additionally, if fireworks cause a fire or emergency response the person responsible will be held
financially responsible for the cost of fire suppression, emergency medical services, law
enforcement response, evacuation, and any related damages to the extent permitted by law.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Increased risk of
wildland and structure fires, serious injuries or fatalities to residents, visitors, pets and
emergency responders, Property damage to homes, businesses, vehicles, docks, and
surrounding natural areas.
 FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implementation of City Council direction.

  AN ORDINANCE OF THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF AVALON
  PROHIBITING THE USE, POSSESSION, SALE, AND DISCHARGE OF
  FIREWORKS WITHIN THE CITY OF AVALON

  WHEREAS, the California Legislature has declared in Government Code Section
51175, subdivision (a): (1) that fires are extremely costly, not only to property owners and
residents, but also to local agencies; (2) that fires pose a serious threat to the preservation
of public peace, health, and safety; (3) that it is necessary that cities, counties, special
districts, state agencies, and federal agencies work together to bring raging fires under
control; and (4) that preventative measures are needed to ensure the preservation of the
public peace, health, and safety; and

  WHEREAS, California Government Code Section 51178 requires the California
Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (‘CalFire”) to periodically identify,
recommend, and map fire hazard areas statewide, referred to as” Fire Hazard Severity
Zones” (“FHSZ”); and

  WHEREAS, the FHSZ Map depicts the entire City to be in a Very High Fire Hazard
Severity Zone; and

  WHEREAS, the use, possession, sale, and discharge of fireworks within the City
poses a significant threat to public health, safety, and welfare due to the City’s unique
island environment, wildfire risk, limited emergency access, and dense residential and
visitor populations; and

  WHEREAS, prohibiting fireworks is necessary to reduce the risk of fires, injuries,
and disturbances to residents, visitors, wildlife, and emergency services personnel.

NOW THEREFORE, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF AVALON DOES ORDAIN
AS FOLLOWS:

Section 1. The City Council hereby finds that the foregoing recitals are true and correct
and are incorporated herein as substantive findings of this Ordinance.
Section 2. Title 4, Section 4-16 Fireworks is hereby added to the City’s Municipal Code
and will read as follows:

  4-1 6.01 Purpose and Findings
  —

  The use, possession, sale, and discharge of fireworks within the City of Avalon
  pose a significant threat to public health, safety, and welfare due to the City’s
  unique island environment, wildfire risk, limited emergency access, and dense
  residential and visitor populations.

  Prohibiting fireworks is necessary to reduce the risk of fires, injuries, and disturb
  ances to residents, visitors, wildlife, and emergency services personnel.
 4-16.02 Definition
  —

As used in this Chapter “fireworks” means and includes:
  (1) Any combustible or explosive composition or any substance or combi
  nation of substances or articles prepared for the purpose of producing a
  visible or an audible effect by combustion, explosion, deflagration or det
  onation, whether manufactured, homemade or improvised;
  (2) Fireworks classified by the State Fire Marshal as “dangerous fireworks”
  and as “safe and sane fireworks” pursuant to Health and Safety Code Sec
  tions 12561 and 12562;
  (3) Any pyrotechnic devices for which the State Fire Marshal requires a
  license to manufacture, sell, transport or operate; and
  (4) Firecrackers, torpedoes, skyrockets, roman candles, cherry bombs,
  sparklers, chasers, snakes or other fireworks of like or similar construction
  and any fireworks containing any explosive or flammable compound or
  substance.

4-16.03 Fireworks Prohibited
  —

It shall be unlawful for any person to use, give, possess, sell, offer for sale, store,
ignite, discharge, or otherwise cause to explode any fireworks within the City of
Avalon unless a permit authorizing such possession, sale, use or discharge has
been issued by the Fire Chief to the person or responsible party using, selling, or
discharging or found in possession of said fireworks, and unless such person is in
possession of a valid pyrotechnic operator’s license issued by the Office of the
State Fire Marshal.
4-16.04 Penalties
  —

Whenever a peace officer charged with the enforcement of any provision of the
Municipal Code determines that a violation of this chapter has occurred, the
peace officer shall have the authority to issue an administrative citation to any
person responsible for the violation.
Whenever a peace officer charged with the enforcement of this chapter deter
mines that a violation of the chapter has occurred, the peace officer may issue an
administrative citation for each violation found to have occurred.
Citations issued pursuant to this chapter shall carry administrative fines as fol
lows:
  $250 for the first and subsequent violations of having “safe and sane”
  fireworks

  $500 for the first and subsequent violations involving the possession of
  illegal fireworks

  $500 for the violations involving the discharge of fireworks within the city
  limits of Avalon
   $1 000 for violations involving the discharge of fireworks in the Very High
  Fire Severity Zone

  4-16.05 Cost Recovery
  —

  Any person responsible for a fire, emergency response, or public safety incident
  resulting from the use or discharge of fireworks may be held financially
  responsible for the costs of fire suppression, emergency medical services, law
  enforcement response, evacuation, and related damages to the
  extent permitted by law.

Section E  —  Work Plan
Davis Farr LLP plans and conducts our engagements in the most efficient manner possible, and our audit approach
is unique with regard to the following:
  •  Our firm is sensitive to the priorities and work requirements of our clients. We work around the schedules
  of our clients when scheduling segments of the audit or requesting documentation in order to minimize
  disruption of the City’s staff and to complete the audit in a timely manner.
  •  Whenever possible, we use accounting support already prepared by the City’s staff to avoid duplication or
  unnecessary requests for audit support schedules. Typically, we request support for balance sheet items,
  the year ending trial balance and cash and long-term debt confirmations.
  •  Our firm’s expertise is in governmental auditing. Our auditors are GASB experts and skilled at addressing
  audit issues that are specific to local governments. You will not spend time training our personnel.
  •  When formulating internal control recommendations, we obtain a thorough understanding of the specific
  circumstances at the City to provide a tailored, practical recommendation.
  •  Throughout the year we are a resource to our clients in providing accounting advice, researching technical
  questions and helping with other problems as they arise.
Audit Software We utilize CaseWare audit software for the electronic copy of the City’s workpapers. We have the
  -

ability to accept audit documentation in either hard copy or electronic format. CaseWare allows us the ability to
import trial balances that can be provided in either excel or a text document. Some of the benefits of using
CaseWare trial balance software are as follows:
  •  We create our own lead sheets (i.e., analytical review comparison schedules). This limits the amount of
  time finance staff spend creating audit schedules. Our software automatically generates analytical review
  reports by account number for ease of analyzing significant fluctuations between fiscal years.
  •  We can provide the City with reports showing the grouping of the financial statement schedules for ease of
  review by City staff. These reports show each account grouped to a specific financial statement line item
  as well as journal entries that are posted during the audit.
Data Mining Software We have a dedicated team of personnel trained to use special data mining software, IDEA.
  -

Our software uses source data from your accounting system to search for anomalies, such as duplicate or voided
checks, cross-referencing vendor addresses with employee addresses, detecting accounting transactions recorded
on the weekend, and reviewing journal entry postings for unauthorized individuals. The IDEA software identifies
specific transactions for the auditors to review for potential fraud or error.
Internal Control Evaluation Our approach to evaluating internal controls involves observation and inquiry. We
  -

spend time with the personnel responsible for the accounting cycles to gain an understanding of the processes. We
also carefully evaluate your policies and procedures. After our initial evaluation, we identify key controls in your
processes and design test to evaluate the effectiveness of those processes. In the initial year of the audit, we will
focus on the following accounting cycles:
  •  Billing and cash receipting
  •  Capital assets
  •  Purchase and disbursements
  •  Payroll
  •  Investment and cash controls
  •  Information systems

In future years, we will review the accounting cycles noted above but also look at other processes such as credit
card transactions, petty cash, inventory controls, employee reimbursements, contract compliance, and other areas.
Our goal is to modify our audit approach every year to further evaluate your internal controls.

C) Audit Sampling
For tests of controls, we use audit sampling. Tests of controls are procedures directed towards
determining the effectiveness of the design or operation of an internal structure policy or
procedures. Audit sampling is typically used for tests of controls and compliance that involve the
inspection of documents and reports indicating the performance of the applicable policy or
procedures and compliance with the applicable laws and regulations. Sample sizes vary based
on the population and risk-based calculations.

D) Type And Extent of Analytical Procedures
For the audits of the financial statements, we will use analytical procedures as an overall review
of the financial information in the preliminary and final stages of the audits. These procedures
are designed to assist us in planning our audits and in assessing the propriety of the conclusions
reached and evaluating the overall financial statement presentation.

The procedures to be utilized consist of determining expectations for changes to significant
revenue, expenditure, and balance sheet accounts, reading the financial statements and related
notes, reviewing the budget and related material, and focusing on overall relationships within the
financial statements.

Once determined, these are reviewed to evaluate if the changes appear reasonable or require
further analysis. For all significant differences, explanations are obtained as to why the situation
occurred and additional substantive procedures may be applied, and related evidence is
gathered to resolve concerns and questions.

H) Drawing Audit Samples for Compliance
The sampling procedures test the operating effectiveness of an internal control structure policy
or procedure by determining how the policy or procedure was applied, the consistency with which
it was applied during the audit period, and by whom it was applied. We will draw samples for
disbursements, receipts, and payroll when applicable. Each document selected will be tested for
various attributes that are designed to verify compliance with different aspects of internal controls
and applicable laws and regulations. Additionally, each sample item will be tested for coding to
the proper accounts and posting to the general ledger.

SUBJECT:  Catalina Food Tours Transportation Permit Application

RECOMMENDED ACTION: 1. Receive presentation. 2. Discuss. 3. If consensus is met,
approve the Transportation Permit for Catalina Food Tours to be added to the existing
Residential Vehicle permit to conduct tours with stated conditions.

REPORT SUMMARY: On April 26, 2026 the City received a transportation permit application
from Ms. Erin Eubank to conduct guided food tours utilizing one existing Residential Vehicle
permit assigned to business partner Simon Alvarez. The existing company is a walking tour and
would like to add a transportation component for local restaurants further out from town center.

The proposed Residential Vehicle permit would be used to conduct in-town tours and tours into
the interior as outlined in the map attached between the hours of 9:00 am and 7:00 pm with the
primary pick-up and drop-off at the intersection of Metropole and Crescent in the Passenger
Loading Zone. Additional drop-off locations include Descanso Beach Club, Buffalo Nickel,
Avalon Smokehouse, Sand Trap, and Airport in the Sky (pending approval).

Avalon Municipal Code Section (AMC) §5-14.04 requires a hearing before the City Council to
determine whether a transportation permit should be approved ensuring:
  • The applicant has presented facts demonstrating a necessity for the requested vehicle(s).
  • The requested vehicle(s) is appropriate for the intended use and necessary, for the proper
  functioning of the applicant’s enterprise.
  • The requested vehicle(s) will not have a deleterious impact on traffic congestion, traffic
  safety, noise, or air pollution.
  • In view of the size and nature of the streets of the City and the character of the City itself,
  the requested vehicle(s) will not have a deleterious impact on the public health, safety,
  and welfare.
  • There is no more suitable alternative vehicle than the vehicle(s) requested by the
  applicant that can satisfy its requirements.

If approved by the City Council, staff recommends the applicant must additionally meet the
following conditions:
   Agree to limit primary pick-up and drop-off locations to the passenger loading zone of
  Crescent Avenue/Metropole Avenue.
  •  Agree to limit in-town secondary pick-up and drop-off locations to include Descanso
  Beach Club, Buffalo Nickel, Avalon Smokehouse, and Sand Trap.
  •  Agree to limit transportation hours to 9:00am to 7:00pm, seven days a week.
  •  Agree to limit vehicle parking to a maximum of 5 minutes to allow for the active
  loading/unloading of passengers, never leaving the vehicle unattended.
  •  Maintain an active City of Avalon business license.
  •  Maintain current City of Avalon Residential Vehicle permit.
  Maintain current on City of Avalon Admissions Tax payments.
  •  Provide proof of insurance per the Avalon Municipal Code.
  •  Ensure approval from any private entities for private road use if applicable.
  •  Failure to fully comply with any of the foregoing conditions shall result in the revocation
  of the applicant’s transportation permit.

Renewals to be evaluated by the Vehicle Clerk to ensure compliance every three years.

FISCAL IMPACTS: None.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: N/A

SUBJECT:  Adult-Use Cannabis Discussion

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Provide direction to Staff regarding City Council’s desire to
pursue legalization of adult-use cannabis in Avalon.

REPORT SUMMARY: This item appears on the agenda at the request of a member of the City
Council. Over the last several years cannabis has appeared on Council’s agenda for
discussion or action on seven occasions.

  August 6, 2024: City Council Meeting. Council affirms City Manager’s decision to
  terminate the existing, but inactive, medical cannabis delivery permit. Discussion held
  regarding expanding cannabis regulations and accepting applications to re-issue the
  medical delivery permit.

  September 17, 2024: City Council Meeting. City Staff provided a feasibility analysis
  regarding a store front adult-use facility, the community’s desire/interest in the facility,
  and projected economic and other impacts

  January 21, 2025: City Council Meeting. Council again discusses options for cannabis
  in Avalon and authorizes staff to resolicit applications for the issuance of the medical
  cannabis delivery permit.

  May 6, 2025: City Council conducts a Public Hearing and adopts a Resolution declaring
  an intent to award the medical cannabis delivery permit to Catalina Cannabis, [[C.

  August 5, 2025: City Council adopted Resolution No. 25-27 issuing a commercial
  cannabis permit to Catalina Cannabis, LLC for Medical Delivery Business. (On August
  19, 2025, City Staff was notified Catalina Cannabis, [[C changed to ERBA Catalina, a
  California C-corporation.)

  October 21, 2025: City Council directed City Staff to not pursue legalization of adult
  use/recreational cannabis in Avalon.

  April 21, 2026: City Council heard a presentation from ERBA Catalina  the current
  —

  medical cannabis delivery business permit holder  regarding adult-use/recreational
  —

  cannabis. Representatives of ERBA requested Council’s consideration to amend the
   current medical delivery ordinance to allow them to also deliver adult-use recreational
  cannabis. Because the electorate has never approved adult-use recreational delivery
  and therefore there is no provision for a tax, ERBA proposed a development agreement
  with the City offering payment of five percent (5%) of their gross receipts. City Council
  directed City Staff to bring an item back for further discussion and consideration.

Development of Local Cannabis Regulations and Public Interest in Adult-Use Cannabis

After the establishment of state-wide legislation regarding cannabis, acting in accordance with
its local jurisdictional authority under MAUCRSA, the Avalon City Council began the process to
develop its local ordinance. After discussions and code revisions at four City Council meetings,
the current cannabis ordinance (Ordinance #1163-17, Chapter 5-20 of the AMC) was adopted
on November 7, 2017.

In development of Ordinance #1163-17, the City Council worked to provide a means for public
access to medical cannabis by supporting a medical cannabis business delivery process, while
protecting the City’s neighborhoods, residents and businesses from potential negative impacts.
Additionally, the City Council took steps to minimize the potential impact of cannabis business
in Avalon by:

  -  Requiring any medical cannabis delivery service business to locate their brick-and-
  mortar place of business within the City’s commercial or special commercial zones.
  -  Prohibiting signage on the exterior of the brick-and-mortar facility identifying it as a
  commercial cannabis business.
  -  Requiring extensive odor control devices and techniques be implemented.
  -  Requiring extensive security measures including 24-hour video surveillance, and
  uniformed personnel on site.
  -  Limiting medical cannabis delivery services permits to just one in the first year of
  operation.

At the request of the City Council, the City of Avalon added two advisory measures to the
March 3, 2020 General Municipal Election ballot.

Measure E asked: “Should the City of Avalon expand its current commercial cannabis
ordinance from medical delivery only to allow for adult-use/recreational delivery sales within
the City of Avalon city limits?”

  -  58.45% or 612 voters voted “No” against expansion of the ordinance to allow adult
  use/recreational delivery.

  -  41 .55% or 435 voters voted “Yes” in favor of expansion of the ordinance to allow adult
  use/recreational delivery.

Measure F asked: “Should the City of Avalon expand its current commercial cannabis
ordinance to allow for a cannabis storefront location or dispensary within the City of Avalon city
limits?”
   -  65.14% or 682 voters voted “No” against expansion of the ordnance to allow a
  cannabis storefront.

  -  34.86% or 365 voters voted “Yes” in favor of expansion of the ordinance to allow for a
  cannabis storefront.

Since the advisory measures, City Staff have not received any significant request or call for
expansion of the cannabis ordinance from the public at large. Additionally, the medical
cannabis delivery permit was suspended from September 2021 to 2025. During that time
period, City Staff did not receive any significant inquiries, or requests from the community at
large for the return of medical cannabis.

Options to Pursue Legalization of Adult-Use Cannabis

1. Direct City Staff to Place a Measure on the November 3, 2026 General Election as either
  an advisory measure or final consideration.

For example, Measure E and Measure F were both Advisory Measures that provided a clear
direction at the time that the residents were not in favor of either recreational delivery or
storefront dispensary. In reliance on the results of these two advisory measures, City Council
did not pursue either path.

Additionally, on November 8, 2016, a citizen referendum was placed on a Special Election for
the consideration of Measure X. Measure X asked: “Shall the Avalon Municipal Code be
amended to permit up to two medical marijuana dispensaries and similar facilities, both fixed
and mobile, operate within the City, and to permit the cultivation, manufacture and processing
of medical marijuana products, subject to specified standards, and further subject to a $10,000
annual license tax and a 12% transaction fee/tax on each individual medical marijuana sale
until repealed by voters, and generating approximately $200,000 annually?”

  -  63% or 721 voted “No”.
  -  36% or 421 voted “Yes”.

City Council may request an advisory measure to appear on a ballot as was done in 2020, or
for a ballot measure enacting the proposed changes to the Avalon Municipal Code and
establishing a tax as was done in 2016.

The deadline for a local jurisdictional ballot measure to appear on the November 3, 2026
General Election ballot either by citizen referendum or City Council direction is August 7,
  —  —

2026.

Additionally, even if a ballot measure is approved, it is not clear that Council would be
authorized to award a newly created recreational adult-use permit to the previously existing
medical delivery permit holder or open the new permit up for applications.

2. Amend the Avalon Municipal Code and Direct City Staff and City Attorney to Draft a
  Development Agreement with the Existing Permit Holder
 ERBA has proposed City Council amend Chapter 5-20 of the AMC to allow for adult-
use/recreational cannabis delivery and enter into a development agreement setting forth a 5%
fee of all of ERBA’s gross sales to be remitted to the City annually.

The City Council may amend the AMC; and a fee could be established through a development
agreement. Setting a fee via a development agreement creates more risk to the City than a
voter approved tax/fee. The State of California Government Code Section 66000-66008
establishes rules for how local agencies can establish, set, and use fees. An established fee
should reflect cost of services or the direct impact to offset use of public facilities. While a fee
agreed upon through the negotiation of a development agreement is defensible, it imposes
more risk than a voter approved tax/fee.

Further, if the AMC is amended to allow recreational cannabis delivery, the City Council may
want allow competition for such a vendor rather than extending the use to the current operator
of the medical delivery service.

An additional consideration is whether modifying the AMC and entering into a Development
Agreement fee would subject the City Council to arguments that it is circumventing the prior
voter decisions to reject the expansion of cannabis in Avalon as reflected in the previous ballot
measures.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Unknown.

Legal Framework
Though the use of medical cannabis was legalized in the State of California in 1996, adult-use
or recreational cannabis was prohibited until adoption of Proposition 64 on November 8, 2016.
On June 27, 2017, Governor Jerry Brown signed into law a single comprehensive legislative
document that took the existing regulatory framework established for medical cannabis and
incorporated non-medical cannabis regulations. This legislation is known as the Medicinal and
Adult-Use Cannabis Regulation and Safety Act (“MAUCRSA”). The legislation specifically
preserved local jurisdictional authority to adopt and enforce local ordinances that limit or
completely prohibit the establishment or operation of medical and non-medical cannabis
business operations within their purview. The state licensing authority will not approve an
application for a state cannabis business license if the state license will violate a local
ordinance in the jurisdiction it will operate.

The Department of Cannabis Control Medicinal and Adult-Use Commercial Cannabis
Regulations  —  California Code of Regulations Title 4 Division 19 Section §15311,
 Requirements for the Transportation of Cannabis and Cannabis Products” establishes the
  —

requirements for transporting cannabis and cannabis products between licensees or licensed
premises.

Though regulation §153111 (e) expressly prohibits transportation of cannabis and cannabis
products “by means of aircraft, watercraft, drone, rail, human-powered vehicle, or unstaffed
vehicle,” a carve out exits for Catalina within Section (p):

  Notwithstanding subsection (e), transportation of cannabis and cannabis products may
  be conducted via watetway to licensees located on Catalina Island. The provisions of
  this section and other sections regarding vehicle requirements also apply to vessels
   used to transport cannabis and cannabis products via watetway pursuant to this
  section.

Cannabis is an illegal substance under the Federal Controlled Substances Act, 21 USC et.
seq., (Act”) which makes it unlawful for any person to cultivate, manufacture, distribute or
dispense, or possess with intent to manufacture, distribute or dispense cannabis. The Act does
not contain any exemption for cannabis used for medical purposes. Additionally, per federal
law, cannabis is listed as a Schedule 1 drug. Federal penalties for possession of cannabis
include:
  -  First Offense —  Misdemeanor with potential for up to one year of incarceration and
  $1 000 in fines.
  -  Second Offense  —  Misdemeanor punishable by 15 days to two years of incarceration
  and $2,500 in fines.
  -  Third and subsequent Offenses  —  Misdemeanor or felony punishable by 90 days to 3
  years of incarceration and fines up to $2,500.

Federal penalties increase significantly for selling or attempting to sell cannabis based on the
amount:
  -  Less than 50 kilograms  Felony punishable by up to five years in prison and a
  —

  $250,000 fine
  -  50 to 99 kilograms Felony punishable by up to 20 years in prison and fines of up to
  —

  $1,000,000.
  -  100 to 999 kilograms  Felony punishable by five to 40 years in prison and possible
  —

  fines of up to $2,000,000.
  -  1000 kg and up  —Felony punishable by ten years to life in prison and $4,000,000 in
  fines.

However, it should be noted, federal law enforcement agencies have issued guidelines
allowing for state regulatory policies that include cannabis for medical purposes. Specifically,
the Rohrabaher-Farr Amendment, first introduced to the U.S. House of Representatives in
2001 and adopted in an omnibus spending bill in December 2014, prohibits the U.S. Justice
Department from spending any funds on actions designed to interfere with the state medical
cannabis laws. To date, this provision has been included in every subsequent spending bill.

Rohrabacher-Farr Amendment states:

  None of the funds made available in this Act to the Department of Justice may be used,
  with respect to the States of Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado,
  Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Hawaii, Illinois, Iowa, Kentucky,
  Maine, Maiyland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana,
  Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, South
  Carolina, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin, to prevent such
  States from implementing their own State laws that authorize the use, distribution,
  possession, or cultivation of medical marijuana.
 The Rohrabacher-Farr Amendment is vitally important for the City of Avalon’s medical
cannabis program as the surrounding Pacific Ocean falls within the jurisdictional authority of
the United States Coast Guard (‘USCG”).

The City has received reports of medical cannabis delivery vessels being boarded by USCG.
As the vessel, medical cannabis and medical cannabis products have had all of the required
documentation for certified medical use, no action was taken by the USCG. The Harbormaster
contacted the USCG who confirmed, adult-use cannabis transportation in federal waterways is
illegal.

Though, state regulation §153111 (p) does not distinguish between medical or adult-use
cannabis in is regulatory carve out for Catalina Island, the Rohrabacher-Farr Amendment is
specific in its guidance to restrict funding for interference with State permitted medical
cannabis operations. No federal protections, exemptions or guidelines exist for adult-
use/recreational cannabis. When state law and federal law conflict, federal law displaces or
preempts state law. Therefore, City Staff interpret there is no viable way to transport adult-use
cannabis to Catalina Island without violating federal law (transportation of a controlled
substance) and/or risking the federal penalties as described within this report.

The Department of Justice has proposed a rule change to move cannabis from Schedule I to
Schedule Ill controlled substance. The rule change emphasizes the currently accepted medical
use of cannabis, but, again, does not address adult use. If the rule change occurs,
transportation of cannabis across federal waterways will still be prohibited.

Community and Economic Impact

To accurately determine the potential economic impact of expansion of the City’s cannabis
ordinance, a number of factors must be determined, including:
  -  Federal regulations regarding transport adult-use cannabis to the Island.
  -  Type of commercial cannabis facility storefront dispensary vs adult-use delivery.
  -

  -  Locations for consumption. (Currently, smoking cannabis is prohibited in public places.)
  This is a significant factor to determine as approximately 75% of the Island’s visitors are
  day trippers or from a cruise ship. These visitors would be limited in their options if they
  wanted to consume the product while in the City.
  -  Geographic isolation.
  -  Locations for brick-and-mortar commercial cannabis facilities. With limited properties,
  limited pool of property owners and currently no known vacancies in the City’s
  commercial and special commercial zones, finding an appropriate location may be
  difficult.
  -  Additional cost of enhanced enforcement and additional administrative support to
  manage commercial cannabis regulations as well as additional enforcement for
  regulation of illicit cannabis market.

  ordinance. Further, any City imposed cannabis tax would have to be approved by the
  voters.

Revenue Analysis #1  —  Food and Beverage Sales Comparison

City Staff compared the taxable revenue from Adult-Use Cannabis to the taxable revenue from
Food Services and Drinking Places for the selected cities to estimate the amount of taxable
revenue that could be generated from Adult-Use Cannabis sales in Avalon. For calendar year
2023, businesses in the City reported $48 million in taxable sales from Food Services and
Drinking Places. For the cities selected above, taxable sales from Adult-Use Cannabis ranged
from 3.7 % to 9.5% of the taxable sales generated from Food Services and Drinking Places in
the same city. Santa Barbara, Napa, and West Hollywood ranged from 3.7% to 4.8%; whereas
South Lake Tahoe appears to be an outlier at 9.5%. This is likely due to increased sales
activity resulting from its proximity to Nevada, which did not legalize Adult-Use Cannabis until
January 2024. Using 5.0% as the basis of estimate-, Avalon would generate an estimated $2.4
million in taxable sales from Adult-Use Cannabis. Depending on the tax rate, Adult-Use
